utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We note that we are another quarter of an hour late in starting. The reason being the late delivery of the accused here, the second time this week. Those who are responsible should bear in mind that they have a responsibility to the International Community. If this continues, the trial will take longer to finish. We will order the Registry to make a report to us to be copied to the Registrar, to the President of the Tribunal, and to the relevant authorities who are responsible for these delays. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's the accused who is questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me just add to what you said a moment ago, Mr. May, that I was informed this morning that I would be leaving at 8.00, and I've been waiting and ready since 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Torkildsen, may we just dwell for a brief moment on a question asked by Mr. Robinson, and that's where we left off yesterday. As far as I made a note of it, what he asked you was whether you had compared the assistance in 1985, for example, or some previous years, what assistance was given, and your answer was that those entities did not exist at all, so therefore, there was no assistance. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Partly those entities did not exist, and therefore, I could not make an analysis of any contributions paid to those entities. I know from what I have read that there were some assistance from the SFRY budget to certain areas within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it's all about. This question is completely justified, the question raised by -- the question that was raised. Do you know that there was a fund of the federation for the development of the underdeveloped regions? Are you aware of that? And it had been in existence for decades in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about this, but I don't know any details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know, furthermore, that the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina was considered to be insufficiently developed, an insufficiently developed region of the SFRY along with certain others?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know any details about what regions were considered to be underdeveloped, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a whole, was considered insufficiently developed and that it was the recipient of aid and assistance, additional assistance for its development. Now, do you know that the fund of the federation for support to the insufficiently developed regions of the SFRY was first set up, and it was financed 50 per cent by the resources and income of Serbia, by Serbia's revenues?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that if one were to compare the resources which the Republic of Serbia through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia allotted and paid into the fund for assistance to the insufficiently developed parts of Yugoslavia, if you were to consider those resources with the monies it set aside generally in what you are investigating, that this would be a significant piece of information and portion?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically I do not know. I mean, my mandate when I wrote this report was to look into whether there were any financial and other assistance given by the Republic of Serbia and the FRY to the Serb-controlled districts in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under UN control. Now, tell me this, please: As I see here on page 4 -- actually, I received this only in English yesterday. It's your report, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt because you've put it on the record. You've had this document since November last year. So in case it's said hereafter that you haven't been supplied with documents in time, you most certainly have been. Yes, but continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you how matters stand, the fact of the matter. Now, whether the 400.000 pages that I was given included this document here, I couldn't say, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it's been made clear to you that this witness was going to give evidence. We've had argument about the admissibility of that evidence. We've ruled on it. So you've had plenty of notice, and it's not to be said by you that you haven't had notice that this witness was going to give evidence and what it was to be. Yes, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. I just wanted this to be entered into the record, what I've just said, but let's move on. And I don't mind for purposes of cross-examination. It just gives me a few more problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 4, point 15, paragraph 15, you're quoting Ratko Mladic and you state the following: [In English] "Stated in a report in December 1992 that," [Interpretation] Then you go into quote [In English] "'Our army is one of the rare ones in history to have started a liberation war with a very solid material base especially as concerns combat hardware, ammunition, and food reserves.'" [Interpretation] And then you quote the exhibit number. Then you add the following: "Mladic's remark is supported by a written statement made by Milosevic concerning the assistance provided to the armies of the RS and RSK." And then you speak about my complaints with regard to detention, with regard to some sort of construed indictment, but in fact so that I should be handed over to The Hague. But as you have read through all these documents, Mr. Torkildsen, do you happen to remember, and if you don't I'll help you and show you, that those alleged accusations or, rather, as they said doubts and suspicions that the resources of the federal customs reserves were being used illegally, that this could have applied just to the period after 1995 from all the material and documents you had available that the Trial Chamber rejected, but you did highlight this and place it in your report to support the correctness of what Mladic says and link this up to the support that I allegedly provided in this way and expressed, actually, expressed, not provided, expressed in this way. So do you remember in those documents it was the period from 1995 onwards exclusively that was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the period when Mr. Kertes was the head of the customs of the FRY, that was in the period 1994 until 2000, something, if I remember correctly. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Torkildsen, I'm thinking about the period to which this written complaint of mine refers for the unfounded detention. So that's the period that I mean, the period you've just stated. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. I'm not sure what period you actually referred to in your complaint against your detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume I was thinking about the reasons for which I was unfoundedly thought to be the culprit on the basis of the statement you made, and it refers to the 1995 period of time, and it says that it deals with 1995 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know that the witness can help about this, as to what you were referring to. That's not for him to say. But I do notice from a statement which you made, which is our Exhibit 427, tab 3, to the investigating judge that you referred to an investigation against you because it's said you incited officials of the government to work against the law in order to gain benefit for others in the period, it says, from 1994 to the 5th of October, 2000. So we've got that point. I don't think there's much point asking the witness any more about that. You can give evidence about it, of course, in due course if you want. Don't interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what I'm asking him is in connection to what he says. "Mladic's remark is supported by a written statement made by Milosevic concerning assistance provided to the armies of the RS and RSK." And that refers precisely to the period of time that you've just read out, that is to say, after 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question -- the question isn't clear. You ask questions in a way which is not clear for a witness. What he seems to be putting, Mr. Torkildsen, is this: He's putting your paragraph 15 as to Mladic's remark made in a report in 1992 that their army started the liberation war with a very solid material base. That we have in our tab 2. And then you say that remark is supported by the written statement made by Milosevic concerning assistance provided to the armies of the RS and RSK. Perhaps you can tell us what it is that you were referring to when you made that comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what is said by the accused in his appeal to his detention do actually support this. To me it's not exactly clear that he only refers to period covered by the domestic investigation, which is, as far as I know, correctly in the period 1994 until 2000, because he's also making a reference to the RSK army here, and as far as I know, that ceased to exist sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it best if we get the document in front of us so that we could follow the point. Have you got a copy, Mr. Torkildsen, of your documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You should have. Right. You should have our tab 2 which is headed "Statement of reasons for the investigating judge of the district court in Belgrade appeal." I'm sorry, it's tab 3. Tab 3, quite right. Let the witness, for the moment, have it in front of him, please. You have the document, do you, Mr. Torkildsen? If you look at the second page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First paragraph or the second paragraph as regards the resources. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to read that out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "As regards the resources spent for weapons, ammunition, and other needs of the army of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, these expenditures constituted a state secret and because of state interests could not be indicated in the law on the budget which is a public document. The same applies to the expenditure incurred by providing equipment from a needle to an anchor for the security forces and special anti-terrorist forces in particular from light weapons and equipment to helicopters and other weapons which still remain where they are today. And this was not made public because it was a state secret, as was everything else that was provided for the army of Republika Srpska. In my opinion, these matters could not -- these matters should still constitute a state secret but court organs can certainly look into them. These anti-terrorist forces today still carry the heavy burden of security-related tasks in the south of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the essence here, Mr. Torkildsen, to make matters simple, is that the son can't be older than the father. If we're dealing with matters here that you have described and date back to 1995 or, rather, date from 1995 onwards, and Kertes became the director of the customs administration in 1994, you can't place that in the context of Mladic's statement made in 1992. It is absolutely untenable that something that took place three years later can serve as evidence and proof of a statement that was given in 1992 as to the situation that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you kindly make the point. You've heard the statement read out that you've made regarding the resources spent for weapons, ammunition, and other needs of the army of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Now, you're referring to those. Now, it's quite unclear what point you're trying to make. It's your statement, you see, about these things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is that Mladic made this statement in 1992, and Mr. Torkildsen's statement, it says Mladic's remark is supported by a written statement by Milosevic, whereas my written statement or, rather, my appeal relates to the subject that had to do with 1995, 1996, the case in 1995, 1996, 1997, and 1998. So it's the cart before the horse. How can the witness place that as a function of support to this attitude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's very much more point going on. We've heard your reference to these events in terms. The fact that the investigation was about something else doesn't matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, if you can read the second paragraph -- the first page of this accused's statement. It refers to the -- some certain period of time, from 1994 to 2000. Is that related, what the accused is currently saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that his -- the domestic investigation against the accused covered this period. That is correct. If I can also make one more comment regarding this second paragraph on the second page. It is also mentioned that this was a state secret, that it could not be mentioned on the law on the budget. And as I have analysed all these budgets and looked at them, I can't find anything in the budgets regarding the support to the two armies mentioned here. And that also fits in with what the accused is saying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If this isn't clear, then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to us, but no doubt you can address some argument on it. Now, let's move on and deal with another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you used, on pages 6 and 7, I think, in what is again a very distorted light the meeting of the Presidency of the SFRY to which the presidents of the republic were invited to attend, and you state in paragraph 19 and in this report of yours, I -- and it was sent from your side, the complete minutes from that particular meeting, and you say in addition exhibit so-and-so forth, [In English] "Transcript of the SFRY Presidency meeting held on 21 August 1991, contains a discussion about the lack of revenue in the SFRY budget and the financing of the JNA. The president of SIV," that is federal government, "Ante Markovic was opposed to use primary issues for financing the federal budget. Slobodan Milosevic, in contrast, raises no objections to making money available through primary issues. Milosevic said that the National Bank of Yugoslavia should continue to carry out the decisions of the ... Assembly rather than the decisions of the federal government. He explained inter alia..." [Interpretation] And then inter alia you say that he explained -- he explained inter alia, you say, and then you link that up with my efforts to have from the primary issues to finance the army, which is a complete untruth, and this can be seen from the minutes of that meeting, and I'm going to prove this to you now by asking you questions, of course. You have the minutes, and you attached them. You quote them. Therefore -- actually, I'm very grateful for having received the minutes, because I myself can't obtain Yugoslav documents. I see that you can. So I'm very grateful to you for that because there are some very useful things in it. Do you see, for example, Mr. Torkildsen, that in the minutes here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say this is our exhibit, tab 6. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is C4274, Exhibit 4274, C4274, and it is the transcript of the minutes in its entirety from the Yugoslav state Presidency meeting. The discussion that was held relates to primarily the economic situation in the country and even -- let me just find it. I'm going to show you this in just a moment. In the introductory address that was made on page 201 of this original minutes transcript, in the introductory address made by the prime minister, in fact, the chairman of the meeting was Stjepan Mesic, the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency of the day, also from Croatia. On page 201, then, Markovic is talking about the economic problems, credit arrangements, and so on and so forth, measures of economic policy, and so on. And then he emphasis that there's nothing written here about defence, actually. That's at the end of the central paragraph on page 201. So he, too, emphasis that it has nothing to do with defence here. Now, as you have quoted me, this will be like my speech in Kosovo Polje for which I am grateful to you too, Mr. May. I mean, I'm grateful to the other side over there, the opposing side. So I'm going to ask you whether you've read it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know what he's referring to? I think it's -- are you referring to the speech or the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking exclusively about the transcript of the minutes that I have been provided with. They are the minutes from the 21st of August, Yugoslav state Presidency meeting, precisely the same ones mentioned by the witness. And he says Exhibit 4274, transcript of the Yugoslav state Presidency meeting held on the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read the parts of the minutes that's been translated into English. I have not read the parts that's not been translated, naturally. As far as I know, not the whole document has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's your problem. That's not my problem. Because you are distorting matters here, matters that I did not speak about. I didn't speak about the financing of the army of any kind, and here we have the transcript in its entirety. Now, have you read -- first of all, I say that I agree with Gligorov. I use his first name and say Kiro and it is Kiro Gligorov that he is right in what he said, and that I agree with what he sets forward. That agreements need to be reached on economic and social measures and the function of Yugoslav organs, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you so that we can all follow. This is on our page -- again, we haven't got very satisfactory numbering. The best page, I think, would be the registry page which is small and at the top, and it's page 17612. It's about seven or eight pages in. 17612. Can you find that, Mr. Torkildsen? There's a speech by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have 17612 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think there's no sense in wasting time. "Kiro is very rationally said here," it begins. Yes. We now have it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, because this is a very good transcript. So I speak on one occasion. I take the floor once, and I make several comments on subsequent occasion. I say that I support Kiro - who is the president of Macedonia, Kiro Gligorov - and I say that agreement is needed on the minimum economic and social measures for the functioning of Yugoslav organs and institutions. And furthermore, I state in the next paragraph there is no need for us to view the damages, how far the damages are. They are enormous and there is no dilemma as to whether this serves anybody's advantage. It serves no one. There is no dilemma whether anybody has been spared these difficulties. Do we have reason to ensure free trade, something that is elementary and the evolvement of normal financial transactions for these damages to be lessened as far as possible, and some necessary codes of conduct be set which will be beneficial to one and all. And here I come out in favour of economic and social measures. That's what we talk about. And I say I would rather be prone to have the federal government to focus, narrow down its focus. In this central paragraph I go on to say and you can see, it is 232, my number, for the Federal Executive Council to focus on the main economic and social issues and clear up the functioning of the organs of the federation prior to that, that is to say the Assembly, the Presidency, and the federal government. Then I go on to say that I don't share the opinion of the president of the federal parliament who in those days was also from Serbia and who was highly respected and reputed politician and economist, and I say I don't share his opinion that it goes into excessive detail. That is, I'm referring to the proposal of the federal government. On the contrary. I believe that the federal government should provide a precise programme of measures of a social and economic nature, et cetera. And I say that this should be the gist of the agreement, and you'll find that further down, that is, the question of economic and social measures. And then I go on to say without any excessive criticism. On the contrary, my intention is by my questions to contribute to the federal government which was headed by Mr. Ante Markovic. I am presenting a few ideas of mine which are of a critical nature. So even if you now consider them wrong, please prove me wrong. And I make certain comments regarding the functioning of the monetary and foreign exchange system contained in the document that is being proposed, and I say the thesis that primary issue will be done on the open market to finance the federal budget and through monetarisation of economic development through foreign countries. I say that is unrealistic because by the end of the year, the balance of payments will be unfavourable. And then I add that Pelivan is right, who is the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you so we can follow this. Mr. Torkildsen, this is on page 17611, if you haven't got it. It's the main paragraph. Now, it's time we came to a question. You've been reading matters for some time. What is the point you're trying to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to make the point that this is a discussion regarding economic and monetary policies, because I also mention Pelivan who used to be governor of the bank, and I say that he is a professional in the area as well as I am, because the creation of money through foreign exchange transactions will not be done. On the contrary, money will be withdrawn and this will affect primary mission. This is as clear as two plus two equals four. Operations on the open market will not provide results regarding the moratorium because it will -- the funds will mostly be used for for the federal budget. I go on to say that I draw attention to this with the wish that the federal executive council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're cross-examining here. Now, Mr. Torkildsen, can you assist us as to this speech as all? The accused is obviously relying on it. He's saying that this contained his attitude about primary issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, basically I don't really have any comment. The bottom line there is that they are discussing the SFRY budget, and as what is stayed by Mr. Ante Markovic here as well is that the budget is actually the army, because most of the budget will go to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted Markovic at the beginning when he says that what we are discussing now has nothing to do with the defence. Later on in the transcript, there is something about the defence, and I don't participate in that discussion. I mention here primary issue. You say that I advocated, contrary to Ante Markovic, that the army should be financed out of primary mission, and you cannot find anything in support of that in this transcript. I say here the idea to free selective credits by banks, and this should have been done for the purchase of wheat in 1991 is also unrealistic, because the banks could not provide credit without the support of primary issue. I'm not talking about the purchase of the autumn harvest. There were 6 million tons of wheat, and I urged--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. You're to be asking questions. Any comment on that, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Torkildsen, am I talking about support for the primary issue to purchase agricultural products or am I talking about primary issue to finance the army? In those days, I wasn't concerned with the army at all in any sense. And where can you find a single word that I uttered regarding financing the army in this whole discussion? Can you show me that place, please?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget overall was financed by primary issues. And it's not like I can point at specific items. It's not like saying this specific revenue should go to this and that. So I don't really follow. Are you saying that the primary issues should only go to funding agricultural? I don't really see the point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For various purposes it is used. But you are taking out of context a part of my statement, and as a result, you are claiming that I was advocating that primary issue should be used for military expenditures. And there's no mention of any such thing, because this was a principled issue. And as you mentioned it, and you even quote it in your report, I want to ask you now to give me your expert opinion here in public. So please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm, Mr. May, asking the expert, as this is a financial expert who is quoting my words about the attitude of the National Bank -- between the National Bank and the government. I want to ask him a question about it. So allow me to quote, because he too is quoting me here, three different paragraphs taken out of context when I say that the National Bank should be placed under the control of the federal government, that that idea is unacceptable. So allow me to read -- to quote. I say: "Don't be offended because we are talking frankly now," this is on page 235 in the long paragraph. "This idea as you formulated it to retain the obligatory reserve of banks at a low level is something I cannot understand, so I say please don't be offended. But it is a manifestation of a lack of understanding of the monetary instrument called obligatory reserve."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So please tell me, Mr. Torkildsen, if I am opposed to their idea that the obligatory reserve of the banks with the national banks should be held at a low level, doesn't that mean that actually I'm opposing any increase of the mass of money in circulation? If the compulsory reserves are increased, doesn't the mass of money circulating go down? So aren't I talking about the obligatory reserves being kept at a low level? You know what the obligatory reserve is and when the rate of obligatory reserve is increased, the potential of commercial banks is reduced. The possibility of providing credit for them is reduced. So I'm advocating the opposite, not to have the obligatory reserves low but allowing the National Bank to have flexibility to reduce the quantity of money in circulation if this is threatening to produce negative effects from the expert point of view, professional point of view. Is this acceptable or not?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are increasing the obligatory reserve, the money supply should be reduced. That is the way that I view this as well. But first to also to the allegation what I mention in the report here actually in paragraph 19, is that the president of the SIV, Ante Markovic, was opposed to the use of primary issues for financing the federal budget. Slobodan Milosevic in contrast raises no objections to making money available through primary issues. That is what I'm saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where is it that I say that I have no objections to making money available through primary issues? Where did I say that? And then you quote me regarding something else. You just confirmed what I said. Increasing the obligatory reserves reduces the quantity of money in circulation. That is out of dispute. That any professional will confirm. Now, let me read out, as this is a paragraph that you are quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I got a bit lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think what he's saying -- what he said was: "Where is it that I said I have no objections to making money available through primary issues?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is that I cannot see any objections are made when Ante Markovic, Jure Pelivan is discussing the primary issues and that the only alternative is to finance it through the Topcider mint and I cannot see that the accused is making any objections as it goes from the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, I was always against it. If I hadn't been, then the 1994 programme could not have been enforced. As you know, that was a political decision that the budget must not be financed out of primary issue. That is how we stabilised the situation. How can a professional be in favour of using primary emission without control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You quote me in a completely different context. I'm not going to read out this quotation from paragraph 19. I will read it out in the Serbian language, and I'll read it out in it's entirety, not in the way that you have cut it up here.

utterances.text: No. Well, we can read it. We don't need to have it read. We've got it in front of us. Now, what is the question?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not complete. It's not given fully. "I'm just asking myself whether it is possible, and I can't believe that experts from the central bank did not take part. utterances.text: So to understand what you say, you say two things. First of all that the accused was present at this meeting and heard the discussion. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'll adjourn. We will consider how long you're to have left for your cross-examination. You've spent more than an hour, probably an hour and a half, on this document, and we can't waste time. But we'll consider how much longer you should have. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could I have the legal officer, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a further English translation of the document that we were looking at with the accused before the adjournment. I'm not -- haven't yet tied up where it goes to. I see. It's the English translation pages 6136 to 6157, so that's of some use I hope. And the second point is this: The interpreters have, I think, been having a difficult time this morning because although they have in their booths the report of the witness, they don't have the attached exhibits, and therefore I think they would ask probably that things are taken more slowly when exhibits are placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ideally they should have copies of these exhibits, particularly in complicated evidence like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Probably easier said than done with the quantities of material that we're dealing with and the limited prospect of much of it being looked at in detail, but I entirely take the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've considered the time you should available. You can have an hour and a half more if you want it with this witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this witness is concerned, in view of all the documents that have been provided, I could go on cross-examining him not for an hour and a half but at least a week and a half. However, I'll use the one and a half hours I have been given, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, your main point, Mr. Torkildsen, is it, therefore, in the transcript clear, based on my examples as to the needs to include the fundamental reserves, that I advocate a position against inflation and against increasing the money mass? Is that position of mine clear?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really understand what you're claiming here, because you're saying that you're against inflation. You can't be against inflation at the same time as you are in favour of using primary issues for financing the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not supporting primary issues. Where do you find a single word to support that claim that I support primary issues as an instrument of the federal budget? I mentioned it only in the context of buying up agricultural produces, and of course only partially. If 6 million tons, if there are 6 million tons of wheat then the National Bank with its selective credits and loans to commercial banks helped them buy this up. Then the wheat is sold and then the money recuperated. So there is no negative effect in this procedure. So where in this entire transcript, which numbers several hundred pages as you can see, is there a single word mentioning primary issues as a function of the federal budget? All I talk about is the buy-up of agricultural produces and they don't go through the federal budget but are financed by the banks along with assistance from the central bank, of course, and I'm sure you ought to know that as a professional man yourself?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am basing this on what actually happened later on in 1992 and 1993 when the whole of the federal budget was financed from primary issues. But I do not specifically see from this document that you say anything about financing primary issues over the budget. The only thing I can see is that you do not raise any objections to making money available through primary issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's great. But that isn't true either, Mr. Torkildsen, because quite obviously my insistence upon an increase in compulsory reserves is quite contrary to the idea of any kind of primary issue, because the increase in primary -- in issues would annul the effect of raising the compulsory reserves in the expert sense. That's right, isn't it? So if somebody who is an expert doesn't understand this, then I don't have anything further to ask.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do understand the document, but I mean, basically you didn't raise any objections against the use of primary issues when this was mentioned by Jure Pelivan and Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there then either, and that took place at the end of the meeting when they had this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, that I was not aware of, that you were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think Kucan was there after that either. They had other business to attend to and left it to the Presidency to discuss that with the prime minister. But let's move on. As you say that practice has shown that primary issues were in fact used, what I'm asking you is this: Are you aware of the fact that I was the President of Serbia at the time and not the president of the federal government, the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that based on Yugoslav provisions who it is who proposes the federal budget, who deals with the federal budget? Is it a matter done by the federal government to propose a budget and to put the budget before the Yugoslav Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the budget process would be like -- if we start with the army here, it would be the Federal Ministry of Defence, meaning the SSNO who would suggest a budget for the army. That would be passed on to the SIV, the federal government, and they would again incorporate this into the total budget, and they would further then pass on the total revised budget to the Presidency. That again would pass this on to the Federal Assembly for the final decision on the budget. I think that's at least how I have understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't understand it in the best of ways, but let's make things simple. Is it clear to you that according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, the proposer in the Assembly of the budget is the federal government? The federal government proposes the budget. That's a simple question. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read the constitution, but it makes sense that the federal government proposes the budget, but I also thought that the Presidency had a say in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, I assume you know that with issues of budget in every parliamentary democracy a vote of confidence or a vote of no confidence is voted to the government. If not, if they get a vote of no confidence, the government tenders its resignation. The government is no longer able to function if somebody proposes a budget which the government does not accept, and that is the case in each and every country.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now take a look at Exhibit C324, your own exhibit. And the date is September 1991. That is to say after these meetings and after this quite correct reaction on the part of both Markovic and Pelivan that primary issues cannot be a solution to the problems. Does it not say up at the top the federal government or the Federal Executive Council, the SIV, that's its document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 7?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is C324, your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And isn't the heading "Proposal, or draft law" -- "proposal for a new law"?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "Draft law on revenue sources for financing certain national defence requirements in 1991".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a draft, a proposal. So I assume that you are aware of the fact that laws are first drafted, there is a draft law to begin with, which is then discussed by the federal government in detail, and then it is sent in the form of a proposal to the federal parliament. So here we already have the final product, the final document of the federal government which takes the form of a proposal and is addressed to the federal parliament. And what does it say, Mr. Torkildsen? What does this proposed law say? It says: "Proposed law for the sourcing of finance for the needs of national defence in 1991," and we're dealing with a proposal that was brought in on September 1991 by the government, by that same person, Mr. Ante Markovic for whom you say was against primary issues and yet is tabling a proposal of this kind. This is the proposal he's submitting. Look, see what it says. Article 2: "In order to ensure resources from Article 1 of this law," and this is the crux of the matter, "The National Bank of Yugoslavia will allow for a credit to the federation which will amount to the difference between the resources determined by law from Article 1 of this law and the incoming accrued by the balance federation to finance the JNA. "Credit, pursuant to Article 1, will be paid back in ten yearly annuities which fall due on the 15th of December of each year beginning as of the 15th of December, 1993." I see that the interpreters are asking me to slow down. And then it goes on to say: "The amount of credit not used will incur a 5 per cent interest rate per year, per annum." So you can see, that same federal government, that same man Mr. Ante Markovic is submitting a proposal to this effect. So what does the Republic of Serbia and I myself have to do with a proposal tabled by the federal government, a proposal which we have no influence on because in the federal government of Serbia can have several people representing it as do all the other republics. So what links do you see there and on the basis of what are you able to state anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that only Ante Markovic would be able to answer that question. And also, just to make that clear, I have understood that this was basically the reason for why Ante Markovic later went from his position as the SFRY prime minister at the time. In his resignation statement on the 20th of December, 1991, he's saying that he is not willing to support a budget that comes from primary issues and most of the expenditure is for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not turn things upside down. This proposal that I'm showing you now under your exhibit number C324 is not dated December but September. So it was after this Presidency meeting. And as far as I can see from what you say here, because I don't remember that, Ante Markovic, in his resignation, said, among other things, that he did not agree with the budget for 1992. And we're talking here about 1991. In your documents here --

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but this is when the financing using primary issues started. It only accelerated with the 1992 budget which was cleared later the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't -- you were not right when you said that that is why he resigned, because this draft was submitted by him, his government. And he mentioned something in his resignation relating to the 1992 budget, and I assume you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, but this is the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at this note marked C43279, where the service for legal affairs informs the Presidency in connection with a proposal of the Federal Executive Council regarding provisional financing of the JNA until the end of the year. Is there any dispute that the service is informing the Presidency in connection with the proposal of the federal government of Ante Markovic and not in connection with anybody else's proposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is tab 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They are referring to the proposal of the federal government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They are actually informing the Presidency about it, and they say: "The significantly reduced revenues of the budget of the federation, due to failure to pay in taxes, import duties, and contributions by the republics which have seriously affected the financing of defence, and for those needs, the Federal Executive Council in the past period used short-term loans from the National Bank of Yugoslavia," et cetera. And then there is the proposal that a law be adopted on sources of financing through a credit of the federation if it is not possible to provide the necessary resources from the federal budget. Is that what it says in that document?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as this is the legal service, you can see that it has two footnotes here to provide legal explanation to members of the collective head of state. And in the first footnote, this is on page 2, on the other side of the document I received, in this connection the Chamber of Republics and Provinces decides by a majority vote at a session at which all delegations of the assemblies of republics and provinces are represented and which is attend by a majority of delegates of the Chamber. So not only is it the federal Executive Council and nobody of Serbia that is submitting the proposal, but a decision about it is taken by the Chamber of Republics and Provinces which means that delegations of all the republics and provinces need to be present. And that is the legal explanation of the legal service of the collective head of state. Then the second footnote says: "Pursuant to Article 319 of the constitution if the competent chamber of the Assembly does not accept the proposal of the Presidency for determining the domestic or foreign policy or a draft law or any other regulation or by-law which the Presidency considers necessary, then the Chamber and the Presidency will, by agreement, agree on a procedure, and the Chamber will set a deadline not longer than six months for a coordination of views. If, even after that agreed deadline, agreement is not reached, the disputed issue is removed from the agenda of the Chamber and is put on the agenda again at the request of the Presidency or upon the initiative of the competent Chamber. "If upon a second review agreement is not reached within a period of three months, the competent Chamber of the SFRY Assembly is disbanded and the Presidency of the SFRY ceases to exist. Its mandate expires." So all the bodies' responsibilities here are clearly indicated. Draft law is submitted by the federal government, in this case that of Ante Markovic. The Presidency sends it to the Assembly, and the decision is taken by a Chamber at which all republics and provinces need to be represented. Is that at issue or not, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be interesting to actually have an overview of the delegates in the Assembly at that point in time, in September 1991. I -- I find it unlikely that the Croatian delegates and the Slovene delegates to the Assembly were still there, but I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You may not be mistaken, but what has that got to do with what you are claiming, that a decisive role in that is played by Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't Serbia have its delegates to the SFRY Assembly? And if the SFRY Assembly was made up with a majority from Serbia and Montenegro...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. In the Chamber of Republics and Provinces -- in the Chamber of Republics and Provinces, you have delegations of the republics and provinces. So there can be no majority. But let us not move away from this other question, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've just found it in your report that you call a finding. You say that the resignation of Ante Markovic was explained in exhibit, I don't know which, 4911. I'd like to see the whole resignation so that I could see at least the date it bears. He says that the budget for 1992 was proposed in such a way that 81 per cent was intended for the JNA. Et cetera. Since you have that document, may I see it, please? Could you place it on the ELMO, please? Not just this small passage but the whole document, please, if I could see the document of his resignation. Or if you could let me have a look at it and then I can ask you a question about it. I can't understand this. But this is a report. This is not Markovic's resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Read on. You'll see it's a report of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see it's a report from the press, as far as I can see. Now, tell me, please, what is the date? I can't see any date on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's dated December 20, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear that since he submitted this resignation on the 20th of December, that this resignation relates to a period that is from mid-September, October, November, December. So more than three months after this draft that I showed you a moment ago, the draft law on the sources of financing in which there is the proposal that the army be financed through primary issue. So it came more than three months later and is allegedly linked to the 1992 budget. And do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that. Mr. Torkildsen, you see what comment the accused has made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he correct in what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agreed that this is later. The other document is from September 1991, and this is from December. But the issue is still the same, the financing of the army through the use of primary issues, and that's, according to this document, why Ante Markovic is resigning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see on this document that the note for the Presidency of the SFRY, 4279, is dated the 12th of September? The draft law was obviously before the 12th of September, 1991, this draft law of Ante Markovic's government to finance the army out of primary issue. Then from the 12th of the September until the 20th of December, it is three months and eight days. Is my calculation right? Therefore, the practice implemented by that government, that is financing out of primary issue cannot be called in doubt at all. Is that right, Mr. Torkildsen, or not?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct from the document dated the 12th of September, 1991, that they suggest primary issues as the tool of financing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we've cleared that point up. And now, since you say regardless of the fact that we haven't found in these minutes that you have offered as evidence what you say but quite the opposite, you say that it was the practice to finance thing out of primary issue. We see who the proponent of that practice was, that is the Federal Executive Council. And do you know that even after Ante Markovic, pursuant to the same regulations, the federal government continued to be the proponent of proposals for the budget which -- of what became later the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the use of primary issues actually increased. It became much more extensive in 1992, and in 1993 this was as good as entirely financed by primary issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, who was president of the federal government which proposed the budget for 1993? We see that Ante Markovic completed 1991. Then he referred to the budget in December 1992. And do you know that Germany recognised Croatia in December 1992? It recognised it as an independent state. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've read that somewhere, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that Ante Markovic's resignation was prompted by the budget or by this rather larger political issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us then focus on the financial legal issues then. Who was the president of the federal government that proposed the budget for 1993?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in 1993 there were several revised budgets because of the high inflation. So it would probably depend on -- on the -- on a specific time when the revised budget was issued. I mean, it was Mr. Zoran Lilic who came on as the federal president in the summer - I think it was July 1993 - and he was replacing Cosic, I think his name is. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to correct you. The president of the federal government or the prime minister from 1992 until the elections in Serbia in 1993 was an American of Serbian origin, Milan Panic and my main counter-candidate at the elections for the Presidency of Serbia in 1993. There is no doubt, therefore, in view of the period whenever the prime minister, the Federal Prime Minister, that Milan Panic's government proposed the budget for 1993. The election took place in 1993, towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I got a bit confused using the term president of a government and prime minister. So that's why I mentioned Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry, Mr. Torkildsen, it's not a memory game or a test of general knowledge. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not even that important, but it is a fact that Milan Panic, an American of Serbian extraction, my main opponent at the elections for the Presidency of Serbia in 1993, which were also early elections, was the proponent of the draft budget for 1993. But federal president of the republic of Yugoslavia was Dobrica Cosic, our well-known writer. But the president had no competencies regarding the budget. That was up to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you know that in view of the fact that Milan Panic was my main opponent that could I not have had any influence over the federal government of Milan Panic which proposed the budget for 1993?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only refer to the documents I have looked at, and to me it seems like you had an influence of -- on directing funds. And I would particularly like to draw to your attention paragraph 98 in my report and paragraph 102. That indicates that you do have influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will find that paragraph. Let me find it. We are talking here about the assistance of the Republic of Serbia, not about any federal budget. Which other paragraph did you mention? 102 and 58?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned 98 and 102. Can I please elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is stated on page 36 of this report, paragraph 98, and it's an exact quote from this document that was discussed yesterday. It is stated here in the last paragraph, I quoted that: "The president Milosevic stated his attitude that the means for the maintenance of the technical devices should be planned via the Yugoslav army, and he said that he will help in realising it and that he will initiate the Yugoslav army to finance the active officers and the civil personnel that stayed in Krajina." I think that paragraph speaks for itself, and it talks about influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are speaking here about some document. We'll find it later. But as far as I recollect, yesterday that document was quoted. Did you leave out a critical word, and that is the peacetime composition of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Because in fact, we were endeavouring quite the opposite, that is, to find a peaceful solution to all this. And reference is made to our assistance to maintain the peacetime level of the army of Republika Srpska. I think you omitted to quote that word "peacetime." It is in a letter from the Minister of Defence of the RSK, Spanovic, that I remembered from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is the document? What is the document that you're referring to, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it, but I assume it is 4682. I'm not able to find it now here in my documents. But never mind, I will find it. Because it refers to the peacetime strength, and there is no issue with that. There was no secret that we extended assistance to both Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we would be the worst scoundrels if we hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 11 of the binder that we have. Have you got it, Mr. Milosevic? 4682.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A copy is coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph, it says: "President Milosevic accepted the concept." And then it says the number of men which should form the peacetime basis of the army and should provide security on the border. It means that it should be reduced to peacetime strength because all our efforts were designed precisely to find a peaceful solution and for everything to be reduced to peacetime levels. As you can see from the information presented by witnesses, the forces were much greater, much stronger, but it was as a result of our endeavours that the effort was to reduce them to peacetime strength hoping that the problem would be resolved by peaceful means, the problem of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is your question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, is it clear, Mr. Torkildsen, that we are not talking of any wartime situation but rather an effort to maintain a balance and the peacetime strength to obtain a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your interpretation, but my basic point by highlighting this document now today was to -- because you were saying that you had no influence on the federal budget or the federal army, but to me this document indicates the opposite, because it is stated here that he will initiate the Yugoslav army to finance the active officers and the civil personnel that stayed in Krajina, and that, at least to me, indicates some influence. And remember that the Yugoslav army was financed through the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite clear. It says that I would endeavour or urge or intervene with the army. It doesn't say I would order, because I can't order, but that I would endeavour, yes. And do you know that even after Dayton and after the war, since you were reviewing the financial documents, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia continued to assist in financing the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The English translation has: "He said he would help in realising it and that he will initiate the Yugoslav army to finance the active officers," et cetera. Do you challenge that, Mr. Milosevic, as a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. That is a free interpretation by Mr. Spanovic, Mr. May, which is contained in his letter. But it's only possible in real terms that I can urge or stand in support of something, because up until 1997, I had no competence over the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, no doubt, will be one of the issues we're going to have to try. But you're saying that this was a misinterpretation of whoever made the record. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that it is his free interpretation because it is his letter, but no record of the conversation itself. It is his interpretation that he hopes that measures would be taken along those lines. But generally, that was our position. There is no dispute over that, that people who voluntarily remain in the army of the RSK or the RS cannot be punished by their families going hungry. And their salaries were a kind of social relief that we extended to the Republic of Serbia. So there's no need to go into any detailed explanation. There was no secret over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. The next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about cooperation between the national banks of Yugoslavia, the Republika Srpska, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a cooperation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is page 14 and 15. And then you go on to say at the top of page 15 that there was a report by Miletic, the director, the National Bank of Yugoslavia provided expert assistance, you say. [In English] "As we read in the 1992 NBRS annual report" [Interpretation] and so on?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you're familiar with the structure of management for the National Bank. You know that there's the governor for the National Bank, the deputy governor, the vice-governor and directors. Four different departments. I assume that's something you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the detailed structure of the National Bank, but I know there's the NBY governor, and it's logical he's got his deputies and his assistant staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to clear this up for those who are not familiar with this. When you say the director of the National Bank, then people would think that that is somebody who manages the National Bank. There are several directors, and this man is without doubt a professional, and he assumed the post of one of the directors. He's not the governor or the deputy governor or the vice-governor. So that, in fact, testifies to the fact that cooperation was on a professional expert level and that expert assistance was provided. So what's bad in that, Mr. Torkildsen? Why shouldn't there be assistance granted?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I am claiming in this report. It was assistance from -- from the FRY to the RS and to the RSK in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say the following: During the period of banknote replacement the National Bank of Republika Srpska collected, and then you go on to explain 12.000.506, the equivalent of 12.506.000 German marks, the banknotes, dinars. [In English] "The said banknotes are hereby delivered to the treasury of the National Bank of Yugoslavia in order to be replaced by an appropriate amount of valid banknotes." [Interpretation] So the replacement of money moving from old dinars to the new dinars. Now, this whole operation, if someone has German marks, for example, and lives in South Africa and then they're moving to the euro and then he has to exchange the German Marks via some bank for euros because the German marks will not be valid after a certain period of time, so where is that operation different from this one? It's a technical operation. You can take anyone. It can be an American, a Norwegian like yourself who for example is in possession of old dinars and he has a time limit up until which he can transfer those dinars. So where is the difficulty there if this financial transaction is being conducted?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it's a technical cooperation, but it's limited to the area of the RSK, the RS, and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Now, do you constantly forget the environment and circumstances under which all the Serbian people lived and all the other inhabitants who are inhabitants of Serbia, the RS and RSK? They were completely isolated, faced with international sanctions that had been imposed exclusively against Serbia, Montenegro, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the RS and RSK. Are you forgetting all that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not forgetting it. And I guess that that was one of the reasons for this monetary integration. I mean, the RS and the RSK were in an isolated area and that's why you had to cooperate financially. But this cooperation was very much of a subordinated nature with the NBY in the decision-making role and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Mr. Torkildsen. You know full well that in trade, in commerce, one exchanges an equivalent for an equivalent. If a company in Serbia, for example, is purchasing something from the RS, it pays the price of those logs, for example, and there is no subordinate relationship. This exchange is done on the basis of the price that is prevail on the market, goods for goods or whatever you like to call it. So what kind of subordination are you talking about? When you talk about financial institutions, when you look at them in your professional capacity you can only talk about cooperation here. They are three financial institutions. I hope that's not in dispute. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is definitely in dispute. If we go to Exhibit C4779, we will definitely see the subordinated relationship I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find that document. 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get it. Eighteen, I think. Yes. Mr. Torkildsen, what do you refer to here that we have at tab 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to go to the second point. There are listed quite a number of points, 1 to 15. And in the second one it is stated there that: "The National Bank of Republika Srpska and the National Bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina operate as main branch offices of the Yugoslav National Bank and under its authority alone." And as further stated in paragraph 4: "The National Bank of Republika Srpska, the National Bank of Republic of Serbian Krajina shall implement the decisions of the Yugoslav National Bank in a disciplined manner." And in paragraph 7 it's mentioned: "The governor of the National Bank of Republika Srpska and the governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Serbian Krajina are required to attend the sessions of the council of the Yugoslav National Bank without the voting right." I think that this illustrates very much that this was not the relationship between equals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, you've just said without the right to vote, without voting rights. So they are not the main branches. But we're talking about cooperation in which efforts are made to keep the same criteria. That is to say, not to reduce or increase interest rates, for example, to the disadvantage of the other side, the others involved, and to adhere to discipline in financial undertakings and financial discipline is a very vital characteristic, I'm sure you'll agree, for successful financial transactions, that is to ensure that clients are not at a disadvantage through the irresponsible behaviour of any one of those three banks. And quite certainly, most of the professional potential and economic potential lies in the hands of the National Bank of Yugoslavia. That is not in dispute. Is that in dispute from your professional expert point of view, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that this document speaks for itself and I don't really have any comments to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Torkildsen. Let's take the liberal economy of the United States. Who topples the prime rate, for example, or raises the prime rate? One of the leading commercial banks. Isn't at that right? Morgan Chase for example. Or one of the other leading banks. Actually, it doesn't even have to be the first. It reduces the prime rate, or raises the prime rate, one does that, one bank does that and the others follow suit. So there's always a leading bank which makes a move which is respected by all the rest. Isn't that so, even when you're talking about commercial banks and not cooperation between central banks as it is here between Republika Srpska, Republic of Serbian Krajina and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the central bank that sets the interest rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you not consider that it is necessary, if it is narrowed down, if the economic environment is so narrowed down to the extent to which daily some 12 million people are struggling for their survival, for mere existence, on a market which has been restricted under sanctions where it has been closed off by sanctions, that full cooperation is necessary to service the limited possibilities that the economy has and that is functioning under quite impossible circumstances and conditions? Is that clear to you? And where is the problem if the central banks cooperate amongst themselves? Is it a crime?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it is a problem at all, and I'm not saying that it is directly a crime either. But it depend on what this financial assistance facilitates, and it ultimately facilitated the financing of the RS army and also the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, I assume you know as well that apart from the army, the Republika Srpska and RSK have their educational system, they have their health system and health service, its public services. It has their -- its pension funds and intervention for social allotments for refugees and so on and so forth. And for a series of other things that every state or even every municipality, if you will, must needs have. So how can you boil that down to the army alone? Well, the people over thereby the people living over there, so many people. They didn't only have military needs. Military needs in that respect were the least of their needs because they had too many arms, too much weapons, especially in this area. So why are you forgetting about the all the other needs that the budget has to provide for?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not forgetting about them, but it is a fact that the major part of the budgets went to the army. And that can be demonstrated by documents. And I don't think that's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's always -- the budget always sets aside the largest portion for the army, for example. But you're losing from sight the fact that Yugoslavia has two republics, Serbia and Montenegro, and that in the budget of Yugoslavia, which is financed by Serbia and Montenegro, the largest portion is set aside for the army. And within the budget of the Republic of Serbia, and the Republic of Montenegro and the budget of Serbia is bigger than the federal budget, there's not a single dinar earmarked for the army. All the other needs are catered to. So do you have any idea that when you look at the general public and joint consumption picture that you must bear in mind the sum total of all these parts of the budget, not only that portion financed from the budget. The army is financed by the budget of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because there's only one army. But the army is not financed from the budgets of either Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped -- I've stopped you, Mr. Milosevic. You're supposed to be asking questions, not making speeches. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that when we're talking about Yugoslavia, the army is financed from the federal budget?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also clear to you, for example, that the health service and education is not financed from the federal budget?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I would have to look at the actual budgets again, but I would assume that you're correct there. I haven't seen anything to contradict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as we said, the health service, education, public services, pension funds, and many other things are financed at the level of the republics. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm -- I'm just assuming that what you are saying is correct and -- I'm absolutely sure that the economic and financial sacrifices made by the Republic of Serbia in supporting the RSK and the RS with the humanitarian aid and so on were great, and I got no reason not to believe that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Torkildsen, I assume you are also bearing in mind the hundreds of thousands of refugees that Serbia took in based on the principle of non-discrimination and it took them in from all parts of Yugoslavia, which is also that invisible aspect and portion which requires an enormous amount of funds to be secured to cater to the needs of those refugees in addition to the everything else. And not only in the Republika and the RSK but hundreds of thousands are in Serbia. So apart from this humanitarian aid this humanitarian aid would come under this heading too. Right? Are you bearing all that in mind?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me that sound like a fair assumption. I got no detailed knowledge about the humanitarian aid provided, but I with just assume it must have been great and representing enormous amounts of money and ultimately sacrifices made by the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
