utterances.text: The Serbian people in Serbia and the inhabitants of Serbia of non-Serb origin, that is people of all the ethnic groups, have taken upon themselves an enormous burden to help the RS and the RSK. Did you delve into an analysis of those facts at all? Who else could have helped them?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not conducted an analysis of that. And as you are correctly pointing out, who else could have helped them? I don't think there was anybody else to help them than the Republic of Serbia and or the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, what is it we're talking about? And secondly, Mr. Torkildsen, I have gain the impression that an atmosphere is being promoted here where there seems to be some sort of secret with respect to the assistance we gave to the RS and RSK. You have an exhibit here. I apologise, Mr. May, but I can't see the number. It's been taken out of a binder, but page number is 00435081. And it is a photocopy, in fact, of the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska Krajina, number 3, page 205, Tuesday the 25th of April, 1993, is the date. It's your exhibit, but it has -- it's come out of my tab, so I can't give you the tab number. I just have the page number, 00435081. It is the Official Gazette of the RSK. And that is a public document that is printed, is published, and is available to one and all. And this is what it states: "Decision" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Decision on allocation of funds for financing." It is the English translation. The RSK in the period from January until June 1993. 2004356130043/5688. Those are your -- that is your numbering. OTP team 5, 1 and 2, et cetera. And when it says is the following: "Decision on the distribution of the resources for financing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Milosevic, while we're looking for it. Just read out what it is you want to put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me read it out. They're your documents, so there is nothing there that is in dispute. It says: "The funds to finance the competencies of the RSK," the amount doesn't matter, "shall be ensured" and then it has a colon, "from the source funds of the Republika Srpska Krajina to the total amount of such-and-such." And then the next point states: "From additional funds of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in areas under UN protection," and the amounts are stipulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're told it's 64. 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the point is as follows, not to waste time, the point is this, Mr. May: This Official Gazette is a publish document, and it publicly states that from additional funds of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are used to finance, et cetera. And then the other points, once again relying on the funds of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the credits of the national -- from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, because having a credit from the National Bank of Yugoslavia was in part, I suppose, supported by the National Bank of Yugoslavia, credits from the National Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why do certain aspects of assistance to the RS and RSK seem to be made a mystery of, as if we're dealing with some sort of discovery, the discovery of some secret facts which are public knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a very interesting document, as the accused is pointing out. It is stated here that a large proportion of the budget is obtained from additional funds of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And also as he's pointing out, an even larger amount is actually originating from credits here, being a different word for primary emissions, again originating from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. And, basically, if you add these two figures, you will see that more than 90 per cent of the total proposed budget was financed from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And looking at -- it is suggested what this is going to be spent on. It is a breakdown on the second page of the translation here, where we can see that the two-thirds of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- This proposed budget, the expenditure would be for education and self-protection and a part of that would be the funds for military salaries, comprising about one-third of the total budget ultimately provided by the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the question was it was made public at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was made public, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why then this mystification, Mr. Torkildsen, as just we're uncovering what the papers say on the 20th of April, 1993? Do you have the need to uncover or discover anything that has been common knowledge for anybody who wanted to read about it in the papers, for example?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about anything being a secret, then we would have to go to the item concerning National Bank credits, which actually financed about two-thirds of this budget. Because the right way that I have understood this, and I'm absolutely sure that this is correct, is that the National Bank credits you're talking about here, they are here referring to National Bank credits from the National Bank of Republika Srpska Krajina. But this would again ultimately originate from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. And that is not straightforward clear from the document that these credits originate from the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Torkildsen. Let's -- I'm really interested in this. I'm really interested in hearing your professional expert opinion. It's not in the document because they are referring to their own National Bank. And let me add that most probably the National Bank of the Republika Srpska Krajina would not be able to fulfil that obligation had it not received assistance from the National Bank of Yugoslavia and had it not taken out a credit with the National Bank of Yugoslavia, although that's not what it says expressly. Now, explain this to me, please: As we are facing isolation and we were in isolation and some kind of cooperation and assistance was established, where, in principle but just in principle from the professional expert stance, is that different from the assistance by the International Monetary Fund to the country XYZ to ensure economic stability and any kind of stability at all, in fact? Where is that different when the International Monetary Fund, for example, decides to grant country XYZ a credit amounting to such-and-such under favourable conditions to maintain its country's economic stability. So from a professional point of view, where is that different in principle? And who makes the decision? Is the decision made by the recipient of the credit or is it the decision made by the International Monetary Fund? That is an expert question for you who are an financial expert yourself?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think the difference would very much be that the International Monetary Fund, I don't think would provide assistant to an army of such a magnitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, you'll have twenty minutes left, if you would organise your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's too little, Mr. May. Will you please let me have the rest of the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You take up a long time dealing with irrelevant matters and arguing with witnesses. If you organised your time better, then you would be able to get on to the most important things first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the war in Slovenia probably is insignificant. It probably doesn't apply to financial documents but it does refer to other exhibited documents. So I couldn't refrain from the satisfaction of drawing your attention to that but I agree with you, it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered your application, Mr. Milosevic. You can have half an hour more. We'll then hear any examination by the amicus there might be, and, Mr. Nice, we won't start any other witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are 92 bis matters for consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are 92 bis matters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I have so little time, I will cover a few very specific points. Mr. Torkildsen, clearly that in the interest of supporting the positions of the opposite side, you're using an excerpt in your report from a speech of the commander of the staff of the army of Republika Srpska from September 1992, and it is B5507. So what should conform -- confirm the allegations of the opposite side. It is on page 0104299, and it says in part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Our army is among the few in history which started a liberation war with a very sound material base particularly with regard to material Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. equipment, food reserves, and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the quote. I can't exactly see it there, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help me with this, please: Whereabouts is it in the document, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since I received from the party opposite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We want to find the passage. Mr. Nice, can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll find it then. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as these are also financial, economic aspects of what you are quoting here, why didn't you include in your report the rest of what is stated there, the very next sentence in which Mladic says, and I'm quoting now -- you can take the document, Mr. May, and check it for yourself. The document is tab 2. It is the report of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, submitted by Ratko Mladic. I received it from you. And he says: "A large part of that, and especially food and fuel, in addition to the army, is being used by the civilian population and its institutions. According to rough estimates, the army with its material reserves is financing 20 per cent of the civilian population. But it should be the other way around. It's the people who should finance the army. Of course, such a situation will is not prevail for long because reserves are running out."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 5 at the bottom or.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness find it. Have you got it, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it is on page 5? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 5 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraph started with "Logistic security"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, Mr. Torkildsen, what is the financial effect or the monetary or economic component? You see in this fact that the army is supporting a large proportion of the population, maintaining it, keeping it alive in Republika Srpska precisely on the basis of the material possibilities that it had at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the consequence would be less resources for the army if they are using of their own resources to feed the population. That's the only logical answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you include in your report the statements from paragraph 1, page 01042298, in which he says: "In accordance with the law on the army, the Presidency of the Serbian Republic in June this year decided to form, organise, and establish the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I'm looking at financial matters. I mean, I haven't included every quote that's mentioned in every document that I have submitted. But that's why I submitted the documents in full as attachments. Of course there could be other parts of these documents that are of interest and of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you did not speak only about the support and assistance sent to Republika Srpska in financial terms, but you also mentioned in manpower, professional cadres, et cetera, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then tell me, why didn't you incorporate in your report, as you did mention this, the first and second paragraph of this same report on page marked 01042299, where it says: "A problem in its own right is the lack of active-duty officers in the army. Out of the total number of officers, Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina, our army has so far been joined only by --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what is the reference, please, page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 5, or 18132, paragraph at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it says: "Out of the total number of Serbian officers native to Bosnia-Herzegovina, only about 21.3 per cent have joined our army so far." In brackets it says: "There were 4.206 and only 900 came over. That is one-half of the establishment needs of the army." And in the next paragraph is says: Although those 21 per cent of officers of the former JNA joined our army from patriotic and the most humane reasons, and it is indisputable that they have reorganised the army with their expertise and sacrifice thus freeing Serbian territories, they have often fallen victim to individuals lacking awareness or even organised groups whose primary aim in this war is personal gain without regard for the defence of the Serbian people." So you've seen that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where in these statements, I've quoted several now, is it possible even to discern or find any clue of the existence of a plan or a financial construction or any aid in officer cadres when it is quite visible that only 21 per cent of the total officer staff joined from among the ranks of the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina who used to be officers of the JNA before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you asked to look into that, Mr. Torkildsen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I remember. I mean, of course I haven't, as I pointed out, included every quote. The quote that I included from this document by Mladic I think was very telling, and that's why I included it in short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I quoted them in greater length, and does it appear to you that when one does that, then what you wanted to attribute to those quotations taken out of context is lost.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. I mean, here we are specifically talking about the officers in the army. But as I understood what I quoted in the report, here is also referring to all the material and equipment that was left by the JNA when they pulled out of Bosnia and that this material and equipment was used by the newly-formed VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Torkildsen, have as your assignment or did it occur to you to analyse the material and equipment which was left behind after the withdrawal of the JNA in territories controlled by Croatian forces, Muslim forces? Not just in weapons and equipment but entire military factories manufacturing explosives, various other supplies for the army. And they also were left behind, though they were the property of the former JNA, and they remained in territories under control of the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you examine that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was it part of your assignment to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not, because the way I understood it was that that would not directly be part of the -- of any evidence relative to the indictment of the accused. And further, I haven't seen any evidence, as far as I know, to the respect of that. Whether any quantities of equipment, material, et cetera, were left by the JNA for Croat or Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You hadn't heard of the takeover of entire brigades and corps and their equipment, weapons, ammunition factories, military factories, airports, and everything else that was in the possession of the JNA and was left behind in those territories? You had none of that in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really haven't touched anything so it can't be my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not looked at that aspect, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please read now paragraph 3 on the page marked 01042296 of this same report when it says: "By decisions of the --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're not going to find this. We've got different pagination. Can you help, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was very early on but if the accused reads out the first line we'll probably get that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go on reading Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By decision of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 2, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "The decisions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska of the 12th of May 1992 enabled, provided the conditions for the armed people, the Serbs in the former JNA and the available material and equipment to be used to transform the units and form the army of Republika Srpska." Since, therefore, you say that you analysed the financial aspects of the military documents, does it follow from this an answer to the question as to who created the army of Republika Srpska? Was it somebody in Serbia or in SFRY or in FRY, or is it quite clear from this quote how the army of Republika Srpska was formed? And also from the standpoint of the finances of the military documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- What are the financial consequences of those documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there. The first question is can you help as to who established the army? The second one is can you help as to how it was financed? If you would deal with those separately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got no competence or really no knowledge of how the army of the Republika Srpska were established. When it comes to the finances, it's not a particular point in this document that this aspect. The reason why I included this document in the first place was to put the financing itself that I talked about in other documents into some sort of perspective, because of course when you provide someone with a lot of material, equipment, that allows them to form the army, that would constitute a lot in monetary terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But Mr. Torkildsen, on page 03077397. And at point 6, you indicated that the support extended was directed to Serb military units that were established in areas under Serb control in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also for organs of Serbian civilian authorities established in these areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And since you say that the support was directed, tell me, who directed the support that you are talking about towards military units and towards civilian authorities, or to be more specific in my question, as you explained credits, loans, financial assistance, surely the person who takes a loan, who receives financial assistance, is the one who directs it, who distributes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly. It depends on what sort of for instance, of a loan, if you were the receiver of a loan. It depends on what terms you were supposed to use it. It could be that you receive a loan for a specific purpose. And the same thing goes for whatever was provided towards the budget. I mean, I would assume that it was the receiver of the funds that partly took the decision. But it should be clear to the ones that gave this assistance to the budgets that most of it could be used for military purposes since most of the budgets were actually for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you who directed those funds. If the Republic of Srpska Krajina or the Republika Srpska is given a credit, a loan, to cover the deficit in its budget, surely the recipient of that loan and who takes the decision about the budget is the one who will direct those funds. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right that they would direct the funds, but it should also be clear from the provider side of the loan that they obviously knew what the loan was going to be used for. That is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you one thing, and you're giving me a different answer. The credit was used to assist the people living there. That's quite clear. That was the motive why Serbia, Yugoslavia, and Montenegro were extending assistance to assist the people. And surely those people have their own government who will take care of the use of those funds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. You're making these assertions. It's asserted that the money was to be for the people, that Serbia was making loans for the people. Is that consistent with what you saw or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely not. I think that one of the -- let's take, for instance, the -- the revised budget for the Republika Srpska in 1993. It's a very good example of what the use of the money was for. And I mean, its an obvious for the provider of the money, meaning here the FRY, that when more than 90 per cent of the budget is for the army, it's not only for the good of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you do not believe it is in the interest of the people for lives to be protected if the people are attacked but only thing that have nothing to do with protection and defence?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I always think that the budget should be a mixed picture, but I also think that is rather telling in terms of the priority was given when more than 90 per cent of the money in the budget is actually given to the army. I mean, how much would that be left for schooling, hospitals, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Torkildsen. Let us move on to be even more precise about certain matters. Was it unconsciously or unintentionally that you omitted to mention medical aid, aid in medicines, sanitary supplies, assistance in doctors as a certain expert profile that helped the most in taking care of what was most in jeopardy and that is the health of the people. And many doctors went to help their people in the areas of the RS and the RSK. Do you consider that also, that is medical aid, medicines, sanitary supplies, foodstuffs, and all other material and financial assistance, did you analyse all those forms of assistance as well?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, basically because I don't think it's very relevant to the case whether they received medical aid and so on. As I mentioned before, I'm sure that your sacrifices in terms of providing humanitarian aid were great, but I don't know how relevant it is to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that in -- under paragraph 8 you say that the aid varied in the period from 1991 to 1995, tell me, according to your findings, when was it highest? When was it less intensive, and in what period was it more in the form of financial aid and less in material aid? So could you please break that down and convey any conclusions that you made regarding those time periods? I'd like to hear that from you.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to do my best. In my view, the financial assistance seemed to be very much on an ad hoc basis. I note that systematically in the year -- in 1991, as we can see, there were numerous requests coming for financial and material assistance through the Serbian Ministry of Defence. And then when we move into 1992 and the entities of the RS and the RSK were established, and when they finally managed to get their budgets together, then it seemed like this was much more in a planned and consistent manner. To me, it seemed like a lot of the assistance was provided for directly into the budgets. But of course in 1991, no budgets existed for those entities. And I think that assistance into the budget was at its greatest in 1992 and in 1993. And at least from what I can see, when we moved into 1994, when the printing of money, basically the primary issues were put to an end in January 1994, then obviously the assistance that the RSK and the RS received through primary issues were less than they had been before. I have to point out that I have not located any of the -- or seen any of the budgets or annual accounts for the RS in 1994 and 1995, so I can't really comment on what they received through primary issues in that period. I have seen the RSK budget for 1994 that I think was tendered through Milan Babic that he commented on during his testimony. And in that budget, there are a proportion originating from primary issues but it was much smaller than it had been previously. But as far as I know and that the accused pointed out as well Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. today is that the assistance given by paying the officers of the RSK army and the RS army continued during that period. And as far as I know, it only ended in the year 2002. I hope that was of some kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is of assistance, even greater assistance than may appear to you. Do you know that after the Dayton Accords in 1995, November 1995, there was absolutely no conflicts, not even individual incidents anywhere in the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got no knowledge regarding that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us assume that it is so. Let us go on the assumption that that is so. And just now, you said that up until 2002, Yugoslavia extended material aid to officers, that is, the army of Republika Srpska. Isn't that fact in itself sufficient for you as a financial expert to draw the conclusion that that was not in the service of any kind of war but simply in the service of the maintenance of the army within the frameworks and conditions within which it was defined by the Dayton Accords? No one was waging war after the signing of the Dayton Accords. And for another seven years, the aid continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Did you study these things after the time of the Dayton Accords in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't. When I'm referring to the financing of the officers in the Republika Srpska after 1995, I rely on press articles, and it is sort of common knowledge that FRY continued to finance those officers out of the FRY budget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, your time is now coming up, but you can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that I have to be restricted to such a degree, but let me just try and ask a broader question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't get the answer to my question. You stated that the aid continued until 2002 from the FRY to the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And again, it's based on press articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for seven years after the end of the war. Is it possible then to claim that that was intended for war purposes?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question I can't really answer what was the intention of continuing to finance them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May, this is within the framework of one and the same question and I have another one after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that within the framework of the peace arrangement, primarily Dayton, the obligation was established to limit weapons and military effectives in the whole region? And this applied to both the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to Bosnia and Herzegovina separately to Republika Srpska, the Muslim-Croat federation, Croatia, and so on? And do you know that following instructions of the international control commissions, the FRY fully abided by its obligations regarding military effectives and everything else? It fully complied with those restrictions. Did you have those facts in mind when preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the details of the Dayton Agreement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you know nothing about that. Is that related to the fact that you were asked to investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you said that I have only one more question, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Torkildsen, you analysed the aid of Serbia to Serbs across the Drina in Republika Srpska and in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That is the aid of Serbia to Serbs. Did you collect any information at all, any data at all, not to say did you analyse at all the aid of Saudi Arabia, Turkey, or some Western countries, Germany, Austria or countries like Pakistan, Malaysia, Indonesia to the war conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia? Did you do anything along those lines and did anyone give you any assignment to collect information about that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not analysed such data because I do not have any documents in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just one topic that I'd like to discuss and to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Torkildsen, for 1991, you looked carefully into the enormous number of financial documents that attended financial trends in that particular year and several years prior to that and a few years after that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean mainly the period that I've been concentrating on is 1991, including 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: 1991. In 1991, Yugoslavia was still in existence. I don't think you dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. But it was a transitional period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the documents that you studied, did you come across facts and figures into the funds for development of the underdeveloped regions, Krajina, Bosnia, Kosovo? Did you come across information about these funds through which the underdeveloped regions were financed?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember, but I have reviewed a lot of documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the financial documents and economic indices, was it in dispute at all that up until 1991, the most developed regions were the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia? Economically speaking, they were the most developed of Yugoslavia's republics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard that myself, but I can't remember where I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: In all the documents that you examined and in all the exhibits that you arrived at, did you come across any information stating that one of the main reasons for which Slovenia and Croatia decided to launch their operation for independence was precisely because they no longer wished to assist the underdeveloped regions of the country? Did you come across information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember having seen any documents regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few things, Mr. Torkildsen. You've been asked extensively about tab 6, the transcript of the meeting. The accused has taken you extensively over the passage that we find on page 4 or Registry page 17610 about obligatory reserves. A simple question that you may be able to help us with is this: Does that passage affect, in your judgement, at all that which you explained at paragraph 19 of your report, namely that the accused did not object to making of money available through primary issues?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a definite answer to that. The way as the accused pointed out as well, if you are increasing these reserves, that means that the monetary supply gets lower. But on the other hand, when we are looking at this in a broader context, it's obvious that the policies that were conducted later on were basically the use of primary issues, and that's how these institutions were financed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But reserves of the reserves of what to what? The reserves of -- it used to be gold, I suppose, but it's probably something else; hard currency as a proportion of money in circulation, is that it or?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think the reserves that the accused was referring to were the reserves that the commercial banks had to keep with the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But in any event, and this was the longest passage of your cross-examination, does that modify about what he asked you about? Does that modify your conclusion or not?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I understood this correctly, it not -- modifies the conclusion, but the result in the end is the use of primary issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We're just concerned with that meeting at this stage and his representations of it. In the budget did you find any evidence of income other than that which came from the sources you've identified of the RS or the RSK? It's been suggested by the accused that they had income of their own.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, it depends on what area we are talking about. In the RS budget for 1992 or, actually, the annual accounts for 1992, they had some original income. But most of the -- these annual accounts came from primary issues, but they did have some original income as well. But then when we move on to 1993, the period of hyperinflation, I mean, as good as all of their income was from primary issues. And that goes for the FRY as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked this question I think to some degree already by Mr. Tapuskovic, but when the accused was asking you about the republic, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, raising money to be allocated to underdeveloped parts of the former Yugoslavia, did you find anything in the documents you've reviewed where money was earmarked for underdeveloped areas or for the purposes of underdeveloped areas?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent sure of this. I -- it could be that I've read articles. I know that there was something called underdeveloped areas, that is correct, but I don't know any details of what was provided or not provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the materials that you looked at and the way that the money was broken down or the money provided was broken down, you dealt with the salaries of officers and soldiers, and the accused was suggesting there was some kind of social relief other than supporting an economy by paying people who happened to be soldiers, did you find any posting of monies particularly to issues of social relief?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's like for all of us. When we receive salaries, I wouldn't call it social relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. One or two other questions. He likened or sought to liken the Bank of Yugoslavia's relationship to the likes of the banks of Republika Srpska and Krajina to the relationship of a central bank I think to Morgan Chase, setting a rate. What can you say to that comparison?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't understand the comparison that the accused was making at all. I mean, the bank he was referring to is a commercial bank and the central bank is something totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, I shan't ask you to do the exercise now, but we can through your documents track down money raised in the way you've described and allocated to the Republika Srpska. For example, we can track the money down to a particular cause, can't we, in the army?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN TORKILDSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think in the -- one of the first exhibits we looked at yesterday, that was C4712, that gives a breakdown of the money allocated to the different cause of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll come to that when we look at a particular cause of a particular area. That's all I ask by way of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Torkildsen, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it to the Tribunal. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll deal first of all with a ruling on the last selection of applications in relation to 92 bis witnesses. This ruling deals with the following witnesses: C1154, 1068, 1187, 1230, 1232, 1234, 1197, 1210. The Chamber holds that the statements of all these witnesses are admissible under Rule 92 bis (A) for the reasons set out in our ruling of earlier this week, on the 7th of April. The statement of Witness C-1154 will be admitted without cross-examination since it's the statement of a doctor dealing essentially with the autopsies and examinations of dead bodies which she carried out. As such, her evidence does not deal with the crucial or live issue between the parties. The statement of Witness C-1187 will also be admitted without cross-examination. The evidence for the purposes of this case is of peripheral significance and not relating to a crucial or live issue. The remaining six witnesses must attend for cross-examination, also for the reasons set out in our ruling of the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll make a start on the next selection of witnesses. We won't be able to finish today, and we'll simply hear the Prosecution on those that we can in the time available. We were going to start with 1072 and 1073. They both deal, according to my notes, with the attack on the village of Skabrnja. 1072 also gives evidence or makes a statement about the murder of his parents, about the destruction and looting in the village. And 1073, I have a note, gives some direct evidence concerning Mladic, visits by him either to the village or to Knin. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, perhaps you could expand on that if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I have to say I will only be here today, and next week I will not be available. Therefore, I would like to address if possible all the witnesses, and I have actually to make a distinction between the two witnesses that you mentioned right now and also some others. We have altogether four witnesses who will mention either Mladic or Seselj, that is members of the joint criminal enterprise, and the position of the Prosecution is so far, concrete example C-1073, in the last paragraph speaks about Mladic, and we think that this paragraph needs to be live, live evidence of the witness, and the rest should be 92 bis. That same applies to the Witness C-1102, who also refers to Mladic and his visits to a detention facility. And that's actually page 4, first paragraph and the last paragraph of this witness statement. And we would also say that these two paragraphs should be live evidence, the rest 92 bis. Further on, the same applies to C-1166. That is a witness dealing with the attack on Skabrnja and refers to Mladic and his participation in this attack and his actions on page 3 of his statement and page 5 of the statement, and our proposal would be to have this again live and the rest 92 bis. And there is the witness 1186, referring to what occurred in Vocin. And this witness also refers to a member of the joint criminal enterprise, that is Seselj and his presence in Vocin at the time. And this sequence should also be live evidence and the rest 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I get the numbers right. So this is 1073, 1102, 1166, 1186.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And those will be giving evidence and therefore will be available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the other witnesses, it should, according to our position, be 92 bis without cross-examination. And, Your Honour, you may be wondering why we have so many people dealing with Skabrnja, but the point is that the witness that Your Honour mentioned first 1072, is the only witness who speaks about the second incident of Skabrnja. Therefore, he is needed. And the Witness C-1205 is the only witness on our list who speaks about what occurred to the victims of Nadin, which is a smaller settlement attached to Skabrnja. Then a person to be mentioned is also the Witness C-1160. This person speaks about detention facility not related to Skabrnja but Bjelci camp in Serbia, and it's actually a witness the witness Grujic referred to. And he should be 92 bis without cross-examination. And the witnesses -- the Witness C-1192 refers to Vocin but only as a crime base witness without any special reference to members of the joint criminal enterprise. And that's actually all I need to add as arguments of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two minutes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can do it in two minutes because I think the position is clear, and looking at the rulings of the Trial Chamber as we've progressed through this large number of 92 bis witnesses; all save 1192 have a JNA issue within them. And that has been the point that we have been making in relation to the issue of cross-examination. I follow the earlier rulings of the Trial Chamber in relation to details that have been given through the testimony of the witnesses such as Babic, C-025, and following the rule of the Trial Chamber, I'm not going to repeat the objections that we made in January of this year. But the issue that remains live is the JNA issue, although in 1192 that couldn't be said to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're dealing with the eight witnesses to which I've referred to. Is there anything you want to add to your usual objection? Certainly four of them will be cross-examined. The Prosecution have conceded that, but we'll have to decide about the other ones. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I understood the lady to say a moment ago that she had explained, in fact, something which I hear for the first time, that there was some sort of camp in Serbia. She says some camp called Bjelci in Serbia, as I understood it, and she even goes on to propose that I do not cross-examine that particular witness. I think that is untenable, because we're looking at a phenomenon here which must be investigated and cross-examined. As far as my relationship goes towards 92 bis, my attitude to that, I don't know how to state it in more categorical terms than I have done, more energetically to protest against the use at all of a type of testimony in this form or written testimony in this form which serves as a screen, a smoke screen, to present an even greater number of false testimony and also to restrict my time for cross-examination, both, and I am energetically opposed to that. And in this particular concrete case witness, I am flabbergasted by the idea that anybody has mentioned an alleged camp in Serbia and then to go on to say that the witness need not be cross-examine but that his written statement should be taken and that the Court should move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we. We will consider these submissions. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very briefly. It relates to protection. 30 seconds in closed section if I may.
